newsitem.title: USA: GE to pay $875 million for engine upkeep companies.
newsitem.headline: GE to pay $875 million for engine upkeep companies.

text.p: General Electric Co. said Monday it agreed to pay $875 million for Greenwich Air Services Inc. and UNC Inc., two providers of jet engine maintenance services that agreed to merge last month.
The acquisition will give GE, whose GE Engine Services unit already provides $2.3 billion a year in jet engine maintenance, another $1.8 billion in annual revenues from the business.
GE agreed to pay GE stock and cash valued at $530 million, or $31 a share, for each share of Greenwich Air Services and another $345 million, or $15 a share, for each share of UNC.
Industry analysts said the deal would eventually boost GE's earnings, because servicing aircraft engines is more profitable than building them.
They also said the deal gives GE a competitive advantage and allows it to extend its engine services business into new market segments.

"The reason this deal was done was that it got GE into a new category segment -- business jets," said Nick Heymann at NatWest Securities. "You now have GE really very strong in virtually all facets of the aircraft engine business."
Heymann said the acquisition would be "slightly additive" to GE's earnings by the second half of this year. "It will be meaningfully additive, several cents a share, next year."

GE stock rose 50 cents to $105.875 in consolidated New York Stock Exchange Trading. Greenwich Air class A stock jumped $3.50 to $29 while its B shares added $4.25 to $29.50 on Nasdaq. UNC rose 75 cents to $14.375 on the NYSE.

Miami-based Greenwich Air agreed on Feb. 14 to buy UNC, based in Annapolis, Md., for $320 million to $368 million, depending on the value of Greenwich Air shares before the deal was completed. GE obtained the rights to acquire UNC as part of its deal with Greenwich Air.
Eugene Conese Sr., chairman and controlling shareowner of Greenwich Air, agreed to sell his shares of Greenwich to GE and vote in favour of the transaction.
Engine maintenance brings a higher return on investment than engine manufacturing, said Bill Fiala, an analyst at Edward Jones in St. Louis.
GE has been "very aggressive in the pricing of their aircraft engines, which has driven down the profitability," Fiala said. "They do see a higher return on investment in the service side of it."
The acquisition will also give GE a competitive edge.

"GE cannot only provide the engines, but when it comes to making a sales call, they also can deliver on world-class service, and it's going to help them more often than not in making the sale," Fiala said.

GE Engine Services, a subsidiary of GE based in Evendale, Ohio, overhauls and repairs aircraft engines, parts and accessories at plants in the United States, Wales, Brazil and Singapore. It had 6,200 employees and sales of $2.3 billion last year.
Greenwich Air has nine locations, mainly in the United States and Scotland, with 3,000 employees.

UNC focuses on smaller jet engines for corporate and military aircraft. Its Garrett Aviation Services division, acquired in 1996, provides engine, airframe, and avionics services for business jets and turboprop aircraft.
UNC operates primarily at 20 U.S. locations and on 100 military bases in the United States and abroad, employing approximately 7,000 people.
